entry.title: The Buccaneers Played Prehistoric Football And Won
entry.summary: It's wise to never expect too much from a clash between two NFC South teams. They tend to be a form of stultifying anti-entertainment, and so today's game between the Falcons and Buccaneers would normally be an easy skip. The NFC South has felt a little different this year, though, and not because any of its teams are playing particularly good football. What they have been doing is playing weird, entertaining football, and today the Bucs and Falcons played what might end up being the weirdest and most entertaining game of the season. A huge rainstorm rolled into Tampa, Fla. this morning, absolutely soaking the Bucs' field and creating the kind of conditions that would make any offensive coordinator squeamish about calling a passing play. Now imagine how much more stressful that scenario becomes when the quarterbacks at their disposal are Baker Mayfield and Michael Penix, Jr. Facing these conditions, the Buccaneers came up with a novel strategy: What if we just didn't throw a pass? Well, OK, they threw three passes, but none of them were completed. Mayfield's final stat line: 0-3 for 0 yards, 0 touchdowns, and 0 interceptions. Any football game that produces a quarterback box score like that is already a thing to behold, but this one was made truly special by the fact that the Bucs won the game, 16-0. They did so by running the ball 56 times for 324 yards. Bucky Irving and Kenny Gainwell each got to live out every running back's fantasy: Irving finished with 170 yards and a touchdown on 27 carries, and Gainwell chipped in with 140 yards on 25 carries. The game's representative highlight was probably Mayfield fumbling a snap and scrambling for a few seconds before throwing a desperate backwards pass to Irving, who churned through the rain and mud before fumbling the ball right at the goal line.

entry.title: Three More Women Say Josh Jacobs Physically Abused Them
entry.summary: On Friday, the Hobart/Lawrence Police Department released a batch of records related to Packers running back Josh Jacobs's domestic violence arrest in May. The records reveal that while police were investigating the May incident, they were contacted by three other women who said Jacobs abused them in the past. One document describes a phone conversation a police investigator had with a woman who said she felt compelled to contact police after learning about the details of Jacobs's May arrest. According to the report, this woman told the investigator that she was abused by Jacobs in 2023 after meeting him in his house. She told police that she went to Jacobs's house after meeting him on Instagram. The woman claims that when she arrived at the house, Jacobs questioned whether she had come to have sex with him. When she said that wasn't the reason she came to the house, she says he became angry and slapped her across the face. entry.title: Irreal: Highlighting The Active Window
entry.summary:
marking the active window (update here ) so that it’s easy to pick it out from the other, inactive windows. I did that by making the mode line of the active window a distinct color instead of the slightly different shade of gray from the other windows. That’s worked out really well for me and I’ve never looked back.
Now Ray Zeitler over at Ray on Emacs takes another look at the problem and found a really nice solution. It’s a bit more in your face than mine so if you’re looking for something that makes the active window really stand out, you should take a look at his post. The TL;DR is that instead of changing the active window, he changes the background color of all the other windows.
Zeitler found his solution on a 10 year old Stack Exchange post so it’s pretty certain to work no matter what version of Emacs you’re using. The code is very simple and you can simply copy it to your init.el if you’re interested.
As I said, this solution seems a little aggressive to me so I doubt I’ll be implementing it but others may disagree. One thing for sure, it’s going to make your active window stand out. It’s a small enough change that you can try it out—say by copying it to your scratch buffer and executing it—to see if it’s something you’d like.

entry.title: Manchester United And Michael Carrick Are Breaking New Ground In Organizational Dysfunction
entry.summary: There are few joys in sports that can truly exceed a game in which both coaches are in danger of getting fired, and no place does that game better than England. There are no distractions that can cause the fevered punditocracy to avert its eyes from the desperate hope that one (or, in the most orgiastic case, both) gets smoked right after the game. This is possible because a dissatisfying draw can enrage both fan bases equally, in the way that Giants-Commanders sickened the souls of football fans on this side of the ditch three weeks ago. But there is one scenario that trumps even that, and Americans will have it tomorrow morning at the breakfast hour: Manchester United at Chelsea. Two big clubs that are underachieving in their own specific ways, will face each other at 8:30 a.m. ET, and in deepest zombie hours on the West Coast. What makes it genuinely special for everyone is that no institution on earth, in any pursuit, does boss-in-trouble quite like Manchester United. Carrick got the full car wash a week ago after successive three-goal losses to Como (4-1) in the Champions League and Bournemouth (3-0) in the Prem. This extended a stretch of winless results that go back to United's Champions League win over Sabah of Azerbaijan, a newbie team that, on the European stage, qualifies not as minnows but something more on the order of plankton. The first loss was in Italy, in a very cool stadium that overlooks Lake Como, and which by definition is the coolest stadium in Europe because of it. The second was at home before—get this—an appreciative crowd that applauded Carrick when the team went for the postgame salute to the fans. They turned unanimously loud, profane, and ugly as soon as Carrick left the field.

entry.title: Darius Acuff Jr. Is A Problem, But Which Kind?
entry.summary: During the first quarter of Thursday's game between the equally winless Pelicans and Kings, Sacramento rookie Darius Acuff Jr. ran the length of the floor in transition and punched home a sweeping dunk past a late trail from Jeremiah Fears and a halfhearted contest from Trey Murphy III. It was an amazing play, which is why Acuff took a second to flex and mean-mug for the dozens of fans in New Orleans. It was also a live play, and as Acuff preened, the Pelicans ran back and Murphy got an easy dunk, after Acuff's absence forced Domantas Sabonis to abandon the paint. This sequence serves as a useful Rorschach test for the Acuff observer: Do you see Acuff's smooth athleticism, and his ability to produce not only tough but beautiful buckets? Or do you see an undersized guard whose lack of interest in the floor game is matched only by his inability to affect it? Both are totally valid reads of the most (and only) fascinating player on the worst team in basketball, although I think partisans of both positions would agree that Acuff's first five NBA games have been remarkable. Nobody in the league has attempted or missed more shots. No rookie has ever attempted as many shots in their first few games. Acuff sits snugly wedged between Steph Curry and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander on the usage leaderboard, with the sixth-highest rate in the NBA. It's both fantastic theater and an irresistible new front in the Real Hooper Wars; the Kings, in the meantime, are so bad that the question of any of it mattering will be entirely theoretical for a while. This leaves us all free to enjoy Acuff's game and use it as a plank from which to mount arguments about how basketball should work.

entry.title: Russia Is Coming Back To International Hockey
entry.summary: Russia, which has been functionally banned from international hockey for more than four years, must be allowed to return to international events starting in December in Canada. That's the ruling today by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, the highest sport court in the land. But there's a whole lot still unsettled, including a looming shitshow at next year's World Championships. The International Ice Hockey Federation banned the Russian member association in February 2022, as did almost every other sport's Olympic federation following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. That war is still ongoing, but in July of this year the IOC lifted its blanket ban on Russian Olympic committees, and said that its recommendations to individual sport federations no longer apply. Ukraine is currently appealing that decision. (This is tricky business, and I'm glad it's not up to me to decide. Should individual athletes be punished for their government's actions? Or is a ban of Russia's prestigious hockey program more accurately a punishment of the country as a whole? But then, why Russia and not some other war-starting, international law-ignoring countries I could name and/or live in?)

entry.title: Raymond Zeitler: Highlight Active Emacs Window
entry.summary:
https://emacs.stackexchange.com/a/36240/47342, CodyChan provides a few options "to better distinguish between focused window." But the one I like best is highlight-selected-window, which, rather than highlighting the selected window, changes the background color of all the unselected windows. The effect is that the active window stands out in comparison to the others.
The especially neat thing about this solution is that when the minibuffer is active, the background of all the windows is altered. So it's obvious even when Emacs is expecting input -- something I often miss.
I've changed the color of the buffer-face-set background from "#111" (sienna4) to "antiquewhite2" because I still need to read the content of inactive windows. The original color is too dark.
flash-active-buffer, which sets the background color of the active window temporarily. I changed the color to palegreen just because. I use s-? as a keybinding. It's a bit awkward, but it's as if I use "?" to ask, "Where am I?" The function highlight-selected-window works so well that I don't think I'll need flash-active-buffer.
The color names that Emacs understands are stored in color-name-rgb-alist.
See also https://www.color-hex.com/color-names.html, but note that Emacs does not support every color name listed here.

entry.title: Irreal: Emacs Turns 50
entry.summary:
MIT Technology Review there’s a nice article on Emacs turning 50 this year. It gives a short history of Emacs starting from its TECO days. Most of that history is pretty well known to seasoned Emacs users but it’s still interesting.
What the article doesn’t give is the exact day of Emacs’ 50th birthday. That’s not surprising. The early history of Emacs involved the researchers at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory agreeing on a standard set of TECO macros in order to improve collaboration. That was undoubtedly an ongoing process that didn’t have a well defined beginning or end so it’s easy to understand why the exact birthday of Emacs is a little murky.
Regardless, we can all celebrate Emacs’ 50th year. It’s remarkable when you think about it. Very few programs last that long. There’s FORTRAN and Lisp, of course, but I can’t think of any other piece of software with that sort of longevity. There is, to be sure, a Ship of Theseus aspect to that longevity but it’s one shared by FORTRAN and Lisp as well.
Who knows what things will look like in another 50 years but if we still have editors, I’m putting my money on Emacs still being around. Wouldn’t that be something?

entry.title: Irreal: Electric Quote Mode
entry.summary:
Unicode punctuation in Emacs. His post is mainly concerned with the vagaries of dealing with English and Polish punctuation in the same document but a lot of the heavy lifting is accomplished with Electric Quote Mode.
The main problem is handling single and double quotes ‘like this’ and “like this”. Because I do almost all my writing in Org mode, I use the ':t option to turn the ASCII double quote (") into their curved typeset equivalents on export. That’s supposed to do the same with single quotes but I could never get it to work for me and always had to add then manually.
Fortunately, it’s easy to make everything work right in the buffer as you type. You merely turn electric-quote-mode on and it takes care of everything for you. By default it acts the way TeX used to by requiring “ for an opening double quote and ” for the closing double quote and similarly for single quotes. You can make it accept ” and ‘ instead by setting electric-quote-replace-double and electric-quote-context-sensitive to t.
Electric Quote Mode is global so turning it on enables it for all your buffers. You can use electric-quote-local-mode if you want it only in the current buffer. You can toggle either of them on or off by simply calling Meta+x electric-quote....
If you have to deal different quote notation for two or more languages, take a look at mbork’s post for a nifty solution.

entry.title: Irreal: Controlling Where Isearch Starts Searching
entry.summary:
new Emacs trick from Emacs Dwelling. Well, new to me. It turns out it’s been in Emacs since 28.1 so for about four and a half years.
Here’s the problem. When you call isearch it starts searching at the current point location to the bottom of the file. You can cause it to wrap around and continue searching at the top of the file but this isn’t always convenient. As a result, many people always start their search by moving to the top of the buffer first. But this isn’t always convenient either. For example, if you quit the search you go back to the top of the file, not where you started.
Sometimes you want a bit more control: perhaps you want to start at the first match or the last match and if you quit, you’d like to be back where you started. Well this is Emacs so of course you can do that. The nice thing is that it’s already built in. There are no packages to install, you just enable it my setting isearch-allow-motion to t.
You can start the search at any of:
The current point position The first match in the file The last match in the file The first match before the window The first match after the window

entry.title: Irreal: Analyzing Emacs News
entry.summary:
taking some data that she’s collected and analysing it to extract useful information. For some reason I really like that sort of thing and am always doing it myself with my own data.
In Chua’s case, she wanted to know how many Emacs News entries she’s written and plot them over time. It’s a little more difficult than you might think. First of all, she didn’t have the complete Emacs News index so she had to recreate the missing parts by converting the HTML entries into Org mode. She did that with a standard Unix pipeline using Pandoc.
Once she had everything in Org mode, she wrote some Elisp to extract the needed information and put it in a table. From there, it was easy to produce a graph showing how may entries she wrote by year. You can even see the years her daughter was a toddler because the number of entries went down for a couple of years. As Chua says, “Babies sleep a lot; toddlers, not so much.”
Take a look at Chua’s post to see all the code and the final graph. The data is mostly useful only for Chua just as mine is useful mostly for me but the way she goes about analyzing the data is useful to anyone that needs to take some data and massage it.

entry.title: Badore: M-x keep-lines
entry.summary:
+ [ ] [2026-10-21 Wed] project A; 0,5 h; status meeting + [ ] [2026-10-22 Thu] project B; 1,5 h; coaching
At the end of each month, I would turn this list into invoices for my different clients. And since every client had their own specific template and invoicing requirements, I didn't bother to set up an automated workflow in Emacs. I just had this list and a little macro that converted it into CSV and I handled the rest manually. (Maybe today, with the power of LLMs, I would try to vibe-code some automation.)
Now, to prepare an invoice, I only needed the lines for that particular client. I did know about the wonderful function flush-lines. It just removes lines matching a regexp. I was already wondering how to negate my regexp used for flush-lines … then I thought: "Maybe there's a sibling function for this purpose?" And behold, Emacs had me covered: M-x keep-lines exists and does exactly what I wanted.
This might sound too small to bother mentioning. And maybe my workflow makes you cringe. But that's that two things that I love about Emacs: You can do things your very own way. And sometimes, improving your workflow doesn't take a package or a custom function. Just finding the command that's already there.
And that is so satisfying about living in Emacs!

entry.title: Irreal: Variables In Org Capture
entry.summary:
building and using Org capture templates. What’s interesting about his approach is that his template prompts for certain information—customer ID and site location in his example—captures that information in some local variables, and uses those variables to customize the capture for the particular customer.
His two main tools for doing this are:
The %^{PROMPT|A|B|...} placeholder to prompt for data. The %(EXP) placeholder to execute the Elisp expression EXP. ms/set-var, prompts the user for the value of a variable, creates the variable, sets its value, and returns the value. This is different from the %^{...} placeholder in that it captures the value of the user’s answer for later use. The other helper functions make use of the captured variables.
Take a look at Schell’s post to see the functions and how the whole thing hangs together. His needs may be more complicated than normal but the ideas he uses to solve them are handy and applicable to many—even simpler—situations.
I’ve used all the placeholders that uses in my own templates but the idea of capturing a variable for later reuse in the template is new to me. It’s a neat idea and definitely worth knowing.

entry.title: Irreal: Dictating Into Emacs
entry.summary:
dictating into Emacs. She starts by quoting Matt Weber on how he writes better than he speaks. Chua can relate and so can I. We both feel the same way. As I’ve said before, “…my written thoughts are always much better organized than my spoken ones…”.
Being who she is, Chua resolved to fix this by arranging to dictate her posts into Emacs. As you can imagine, she encountered all sorts of problems along the way but was mainly able to find solutions for them. You can check her post—and Weber’s—to see how they’re doing that.
When I read Chua’s post, I thought, “maybe I should do that too” but then I realized that I don’t want to dictate my text. The truth is, I enjoy writing a lot more than I do speaking and I especially enjoy writing with Emacs. Although it’s not always obvious, I do a lot of revising on my posts as I write them and I usually try to make a final editing pass at least one day after I’ve written them. Speaking, on the other hands, feels more like “one and done” to me. I know that I could dictate a post and then edit the result but it’s not the same. And in any event, as I say, I enjoy writing a lot more than I enjoy talking.
I suppose, as Chua says, the day may come when ever encroaching old age, disease, or accident may make typing hard or impossible and I may be forced to consider dictation but until then, I’m happy to continue typing my text.

Quxnet has everything. Boards, mail, photo galleries, links, blogs, an RSS reader, and more. It looks super-retro cool, which adds to the vibe. I don't know what I want out of it yet, but if it can remain "A private network with old internet manners." then I can see it becoming a fun new place to hang out. There are still fewer than 1,000 people there, so naturally things are cordial and sufficiently nerdy and polite. I hope it stays polite, but I worry that with popularity comes conflicting views from people who "We" don't agree with, and once the finger-pointing starts, things tend to go south. I hope it doesn't happen that way. But for now it's clever, fun, nerdy, and new, so I'm in. https://quxnet.net/u/jbaty.
